name: Dirty bulk / lean bulk

card.summary: Two ways of eating in a calorie surplus to gain size: a large, loosely tracked surplus versus a small, controlled one.
card.aka: clean bulk, dirty bulking, lean gains
card.note: Wikipedia describes dirty bulking as likely to add significant fat and as carrying cardiovascular and insulin-related concerns; forum debates are mostly anecdotal.

quick.overview:
Bulking means eating in a calorie surplus to build muscle. A lean (or clean) bulk uses a small surplus with tracking to limit fat gain, while a dirty bulk uses a large surplus with little tracking, often including processed foods.

On looksmax.org, younger and thinner users ask which approach avoids looking soft or bloated while gaining size. Responses range from small planned surpluses to long continuous bulks.
quick.mechanism: A surplus supplies energy for tissue growth. Wikipedia says a sustained surplus can add more lean mass than eating at maintenance, with some fat gain expected, and that a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more fat.
quick.risks: Wikipedia describes dirty bulking as producing fast gain but usually significant fat, followed by a harsher cut, with long-term concerns for cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity. Forum users also report fear of looking fat or bloated.

lead: A lean (or clean) bulk and a dirty bulk are the two best-known ways of eating in a calorie surplus to build muscle. A lean bulk uses a modest, tracked surplus intended to add muscle with limited fat; a dirty bulk uses a large, loosely tracked surplus, often with calorie-dense or processed food, to gain weight and strength quickly [1]. People use either approach to build a fuller, broader physique, and the choice is mostly about how much fat they are willing to carry on the way and how hard the later cut will be [1].

Both belong to the bodybuilding off-season, the long stretch of the year in which competitors gain muscle before cutting for roughly 12 to 14 weeks ahead of a contest [1]. The terms have since spread to gyms and online fitness communities, where they appear in forum threads, transformation logs and calculator tools [6][7][11][14][15][16][17].

In looksmaxxing spaces the question has a facial side: users worry that fat or water retention during a bulk will leave the face puffy, and ask which style of bulk avoids it [2][3][4][5]. Wikipedia describes the trade-offs in general terms, and a narrative review of physique-athlete nutrition discusses the risk of rapid fat regain after a contest, but no published trial has compared lean and dirty bulking for appearance outcomes [1][9].

paras: Wikipedia says the link between muscle growth and positive energy balance is well established, and that the size of the surplus depends on the person's goals, since larger surpluses and longer bulks add more fat [1]. Some fat gain is expected in any bulk, and Wikipedia adds that it is unclear how much muscle is retained through a later cut for the whole cycle to be worthwhile [1].

Wikipedia describes clean bulking as aiming to add muscle with little or no fat. It takes longer, relies on meeting calorie goals every day and following macronutrient targets as closely as possible, and may alternate higher- and lower-calorie days; a typical starting point is moderate carbohydrate, moderate protein and low fat [1]. Dirty bulking is described as a large surplus without tracking macronutrients, often with junk food, favoured by off-season lifters who want fast gains in size and strength and are not concerned about fat [1].

Wikipedia also notes a psychological side: some lifters find a dirty bulk easier because it removes the pressure of strict meal planning and tracking [1]. In practice the two are ends of a spectrum, and forum users often describe hybrids, such as a bulk that is mostly tracked with looser stretches, or a bulk that starts tracked and loosens over time [14][15].

sections.h: What each approach is used for

paras: Lean bulkers want visible muscle gain without losing definition, which matters especially to people who judge their look by face and waistline. Threads on looksmax.org describe plans such as a daily surplus of a few hundred calories to move from 155 to 165 lb without bloating, or a lean bulk after a cut by a teenager worried about regaining fat [2][4]. A T Nation poster describes the conventional wisdom of a conservative surplus of about 300 calories, mostly carbohydrate, and argues that it suits some natural lifters but not all [12].

Dirty bulkers prioritise calories and speed. T Nation members describe meals built to hit a high calorie count, including eggs, beans, potatoes and cheese, as their routine during a dirty bulk [13], and others describe a bulk that became looser toward the end, or rapid weight gain from 73 to 77 kg with leg growth while training with kettlebells [15][16]. Wikipedia lists the downsides as significant fat gain, a harsher cut afterwards and, with heavy intake of processed, sugary, high-fat food, long-term concerns for cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity [1].

General references on muscle growth describe a positive energy balance as supporting anabolism over the long term, alongside mechanical tension from training and adequate protein, without giving a single surplus size [10]. They cite a 2018 review recommending at least about 1.6 g/kg of protein per day for lean tissue gain, with no additional hypertrophy seen above about 1.8 g/kg, although bodybuilders often advise more [10].

A 2020 narrative review of nutrition for physique athletes (Roberts, Helms, Trexler and Fitschen, Journal of Human Kinetics) gives no fixed bulking surplus or weekly gain rate. It reports that off-season male bodybuilders have been recorded eating about 3,800 kcal per day, and that a very large surplus (a 40 percent overfeeding example) could cause substantial fat accretion, with only a partial offset from higher energy expenditure [9]. It also describes rapid regain after contests, with some competitors regaining several kilograms in a few weeks, mostly fat, and recommends a controlled, tapered surplus guided by feedback such as rate of weight gain and fullness cues [9].

The review recommends 1.8 to 2.7 g/kg/day of protein for physique athletes, spread over several meals [9]. These are general nutrition statements about lifters rather than comparisons of lean and dirty bulking.

Forum threads include a user asking about a 500-calorie daily surplus to reach a target weight without becoming chubby [2], a teenager asking whether a lean bulk will add fat after a cut [4], users asking whether to clean or dirty bulk [6][7], a user planning a four-week lean bulk to regain lost muscle [8], and threads on bulking after a cut [5]. Posters describe worry that bloating or fat gain will change their facial look; replies range from advising a long continuous bulk to suggesting performance-enhancing drugs, which is outside the scope of this article [2][4].

On T Nation, bulking talk is part of lifting-log culture: members describe extending a bulk for a transformation challenge and ending it with a dirty phase [14], saying their bulk was not completely dirty but not the cleanest [15], or following a no-bulk, no-cut philosophy of lifting at maintenance [11]. Tools that calculate maintenance calories for lean bulk, cut and recomposition have also been shared on Hacker News [17].

Wikipedia lists excess fat gain, a harder cut and, over time, possible effects on cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity as concerns with dirty bulking [1]. The physique-athlete review notes that rapid, large regain can overshoot prior body fat levels [9]. Anabolic steroid use, sometimes mentioned in bulking threads, carries separate serious risks [1].
No studies found comparing clean and dirty bulking. Related research on protein intake, energy balance and hypertrophy is summarised in general references and in the physique-athlete review [9][10].

timeline.event: Joe and Ben Weider found the IFBB, helping establish the bulk-and-cut competition cycle [1].
A review cited on Wikipedia recommends a minimum of about 1.6 g/kg/day protein for lean tissue gain [10].
Roberts, Helms, Trexler and Fitschen publish a narrative review of nutrition for physique athletes [9].

lore.intro: Bulk strategy appears on looksmax.org as questions from users who want muscle without fat or facial puffiness, and on T Nation as part of training logs and challenges [2][3][4][5][14].

claims.claim: A small, tracked surplus lets you add muscle without getting fat.
claims.believers: Users ask about and discuss surpluses of a few hundred calories a day to gain size lean [2][12].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says some fat gain is expected in a sustained surplus, with larger surpluses adding more fat [1].

claims.claim: Dirty bulking is a faster way to gain size.
claims.believers: Users ask whether eating plenty of processed food and sugar is acceptable for gaining, and T Nation members describe rapid weight gain on high-calorie intakes [7][16].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says dirty bulking can give fast gains but usually adds significant fat, necessitating a harsher cut [1].

claims.claim: A dirty bulk is easier to stick to than a tracked one.
claims.believers: Wikipedia notes some lifters find it psychologically easier because it removes strict tracking; T Nation posters describe loosening their bulk late in a challenge [1][14].
claims.experts: The physique-athlete review recommends feedback-based eating after contests, with intentional use of hunger cues rather than constant tracking, in a transition context [9].

claims.claim: Natural lifters can only succeed with a very conservative surplus.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster says conservative surpluses work for some natural lifters but are the exception rather than the rule [12].
claims.experts: No published trial found compares surplus sizes for natural lifters' appearance; reviews give no single required surplus [9][10].

claims.believers: looksmax.org users say they look terrible if they bloat or gain fat and ask how to avoid it [2][4].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined facial appearance across bulking phases; Wikipedia describes fat gain as an expected result of a surplus [1].

claims.claim: A dirty bulk harms long-term health.
claims.believers: Users who ask whether to eat plenty of sugar and processed food while bulking are raising the question of its cost, and the topic recurs in clean-versus-dirty threads [7].
claims.experts: Wikipedia says heavy intake of processed, high-sugar, high-fat food can harm cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity over time [1].

angle.text: The surplus supplies the energy for training to turn into muscle, which people use to build a bigger frame. Lean bulkers accept slower gain to keep fat low; dirty bulkers accept more fat for speed and an easier routine, then cut harder.
